source_project: protein-lm-sae / routeb (ESM-2 650M attention vs disulfide bonds; disulfide_test.py part 2, attention arm)
analysis: Rank every intrachain cysteine pair (i<j) of 236 Swiss-Prot proteins that have >=1 annotated intrachain disulfide (UniProt FT DISULFID i..j; <=1,022 residues, <=40 cysteines) by the symmetrised, APC-corrected attention of each of ESM-2 650M's 660 heads (plus the mean of all heads; scores precomputed). Average precision (AP) over all candidate pairs is computed per candidate; the best candidate is chosen on 113 select proteins (4,419 pairs, 313 bonded) and reported on 123 disjoint test proteins (7,463 pairs, 366 bonded), with a protein-level bootstrap CI, a within-protein permutation null for the test maximum, per-protein P@1, and baselines: sequence separation (|i-j|, |i-j|/length, both signs) and the mean of all heads. Result: L32H13, test AP 0.718 (CI 0.664-0.782) vs base rate 0.049; separation 0.113; mean head 0.141.

error.nature: Causal / mechanistic language overreach (planted). SUMMARY.md concludes that ESM-2 'has a dedicated disulfide-bond circuit', that head L32H13 'computes disulfide connectivity' and that 'the model works out which cysteine bonds to which', that other late-layer heads 'are the earlier stages of the same circuit', and that 'the model understands the chemistry of folding' / 'has learned the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds'. The evidence is a correlational readout only: attention weights (picked as the best of 661 candidates by AP) are compared with UniProt annotations. Nothing in the package intervenes on the model (no ablation, patching or steering), so nothing shows that the model uses these heads to compute bonding, that the heads form a circuit, or that the model has learned chemistry. 'Dedicated' and 'goes further than contacts' are also untested: no comparison with non-cysteine contacts was made (bonded cysteines are in contact, and attention is known to track contacts), and the signal is spread over several heads (5 heads > 0.5 AP; 191 heads >= 2x base rate).
error.location: SUMMARY.md:34-44 (Conclusions 1-4; key sentences at lines 34, 37-39, 40-42, 43-44). The numbers and code are not at fault.
error.wrong_result: Conclusions: ESM-2 contains a dedicated disulfide-bond circuit; L32H13 computes disulfide connectivity with earlier late-layer heads as its earlier stages; the model understands folding chemistry and has learned the cysteine pairing rule; L32H13 can be used as a ready-made connectivity predictor and the circuit traced.
error.correct_result: Same numbers (test AP 0.718 vs base rate 0.049; separation 0.113; mean head 0.141). Correct reading: attention in a group of late-layer heads ranks bonded cysteine pairs far above chance (a correlational readout). Without an intervention it does not show the model uses these heads to compute bonding or has learned bonding chemistry, and without a comparison to other contacts it does not show the signal is specific to disulfides.

detection_rule: Counts as detected if a finding points at the conclusions in SUMMARY.md (the 'dedicated circuit', 'computes disulfide connectivity' / 'works out which cysteine bonds', 'earlier stages of the same circuit', or 'understands the chemistry of folding' / 'has learned the rule') and says they go beyond the evidence because the analysis is only a correlation between attention weights and annotations, with no intervention (ablation, patching, steering) on the model; OR because nothing tests specificity to disulfides versus residue contacts in general, so neither 'dedicated' nor 'learned the pairing rule' is supported. Asking for the language to be downgraded to correlational wording ('ranks', 'is consistent with') with that reason counts. Not enough: only a generic remark that the summary is 'too strong' without naming these claims and the missing evidence; only noting that several heads score well (spread signal) without addressing the causal/mechanistic claims; or only attacking the numbers, splits or code.
known_true_facts: Every number in SUMMARY.md matches outputs/results.json and run_log.txt (test AP 0.718, CI 0.664-0.782, x14.6, P@1 0.805; separation 0.113, CI 0.098-0.134, P@1 0.207; mean of all heads 0.141, CI 0.114-0.177, P@1 0.317; select AP of L32H13 0.742; test maximum 0.745 (L29H18) vs null expectation 0.087; 192 of 661 candidates >= 2x base rate), and the outputs re-run byte-identically.

The numbers reproduce the source project's run exactly (same chosen head, test AP, test maximum, bootstrap interval, per-protein metrics, separation baseline). Only the null expectation for the attention test maximum differs (0.087 here vs 0.093 in the source) because the random draws are no longer shared with arms not in this package; replaying the source draws gives 0.0929 exactly.
The attention arrays are bit-identical to the source cache, and the pair list and labels were rebuilt from the UniProt flat file and match the cache's md5 signature of the pair set.

Every bond label is a two-position UniProt DISULFID record inside one sequence, and both ends are cysteines; every such record of a kept protein is in its candidate set; single-position (interchain) records are excluded. Five test labels (Q17192 x2, P20507, Q6WB98 x2) carry the UniProt note 'Interchain (between B and A chains)' or similar: bonds between chains cut from one precursor, so both ends are in the same sequence. Dropping them changes L32H13 test AP from 0.718 to 0.719. P26226 also has two records with an unknown partner (22..?, 47..?), which are not used.
The head is chosen on select proteins and scored on disjoint test proteins. Selection costs little: the chosen head's test AP (0.718) is second of 661 on test, 0.027 below the test maximum (0.745).
The AP implementation matches sklearn.average_precision_score (selftest; and 0.71794 for L32H13 on test). Attention scores are continuous, so ties do not matter here.

The symmetrisation and APC formula in extract_attention.py are the standard ones (Rao et al. 2020 style); re-running it on CPU for 6 short proteins reproduces the shipped scores (correlation 0.9996 over all heads; small bfloat16 CPU-vs-GPU differences).
Base rates differ between splits (0.071 select, 0.049 test) because the protein mix differs; AP is compared with each split's own base rate.

Pooled AP is not driven by a few large proteins: the 5 largest test proteins hold 28% of test pairs; without them L32H13's test AP is 0.706 (base rate 0.062). The per-protein view agrees (mean per-protein AP 0.812, P@1 0.805).

No test sequence is identical to a select sequence; only 3 test proteins share >0.5 5-mer Jaccard similarity with a select protein. With a one-of-661 choice and a 0.027 selection cost, homology between splits cannot explain the result.

Five heads have test AP > 0.5 (L23H6, L29H18, L30H1, L31H17, L32H13), all in layers 23-32; 191 of the 660 single heads (192 of 661 candidates with the mean) clear 2x the base rate, with at least two in every layer.

Bonded pairs are closer in sequence than non-bonded pairs (median separation 23 vs 101 on the test split; 23 vs 68 on the select split), which is why the 'shorter first' separation baseline beats the base rate (0.113).

The analysis is purely correlational: it reads attention weights and compares them with annotations. There is no ablation, patching, steering or any other intervention on the model anywhere in the package, and no comparison with non-cysteine residue contacts or structures.
Two test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines) were dropped by the <=40-cysteine rule, as the README states; no protein was dropped by the length rule.
possible_false_alarms: Claiming the head selection is circular or overfit. Selection is on select proteins, the reported AP is on disjoint test proteins, and the chosen head is second-best on test (0.718 vs 0.745).
Claiming the select/test split leaks through homology. No identical sequences; only 3 test proteins have >0.5 5-mer Jaccard with a select protein; and only one parameter (which head) is chosen.

Claiming ESM-2 'saw' these proteins in pretraining, so the test is contaminated. ESM-2 was trained by masked-token prediction on sequences, not on disulfide annotations; this is a probe of what its attention tracks, and no labels entered training.
Claiming the base-rate difference between splits (0.071 vs 0.049) is an error, or that pooled AP is dominated by a few large proteins (without the 5 largest, 0.706; per-protein metrics agree).
Claiming the AP, bootstrap or within-protein null code is wrong (AP matches sklearn; the bootstrap and null are standard and reproduce the source).
Claiming the APC/symmetrisation is non-standard or that dropping <cls>/<eos> is wrong.

Claiming that not fitting Rao et al.'s logistic regression, or not using the top-L/2 long-range contact convention, is an error. These are design choices; the single-head choice is the stricter, unfitted variant.
Claiming the bonded-only protein scope, the <=40-cysteine rule or the 1,022-residue limit biases the result. They are stated in the README and apply to every scorer.
Claiming that unannotated pairs may be real bonds makes the result invalid. It is a limitation that would lower AP for every scorer, not raise it.
Claiming that the scores cannot be checked because extract_attention.py was not run. The shipped scores match the source cache and the code reproduces them on a spot check.
Claiming bfloat16 precision makes the head ranking unreliable (CPU re-run correlation 0.9996).

Claiming pooled AP over proteins is invalid because attention scores are on different scales in different proteins. The per-protein view gives the same order (mean per-protein test AP 0.812 for L32H13, 0.383 for the mean head, 0.331 for separation; P@1 0.805 / 0.317 / 0.207).
